parts: You grabbed that cart without a second thought. Nobody had to convince you.
But when shopping carts first appeared, in nineteen thirty-seven, shoppers did not want them.
The man usually credited with inventing the cart had to hire people to push it around his store.
And when he was asked years later whether shoppers loved it, his answer was blunt.
So why did nobody want shopping carts at first?
Before carts, shoppers could only buy what they could carry.
Sylvan Goldman ran a supermarket chain in Oklahoma. National Public Radio says that during the Great Depression, he noticed shoppers stopped buying once their arms were full.
In nineteen thirty-six, he reportedly got an idea from a folding chair. Put a basket on the seat, and wheels on the legs.
With a mechanic named Fred Young, he built a metal frame holding two wire baskets.
One of the first shopping carts appeared in June nineteen thirty-seven, in one of his stores in Oklahoma City.
His ad campaign was called the No Basket Carrying Plan.
Shoppers said no. According to accounts, men found the cart effeminate, and women compared it to a baby carriage.
Another account says shoppers felt they could manage their own baskets, and saw no reason for a basket on wheels.
National Public Radio reports that in nineteen seventy-seven, Goldman was asked whether shoppers loved the carts. He said: No, no. That's a big lie.
So he turned to theater. He hired models and actors to push carts through the store, so customers could see how easy it was.
He also hired greeters to explain how the carts worked.
Here is our reading. Seeing other people use the cart made it feel normal. The sources say only that it then caught on.
And it did. Goldman reportedly went on to collect royalties on carts, and became a multimillionaire.
In nineteen seventy-seven, he also said the cart would have been invented anyway, because somebody else would have.
Success brought a new problem. The two-basket carts took up too much space.
A Kansas City inventor, Orla Watson, designed a cart that fit inside another one. A swinging gate at the back let the carts nest.
Watson introduced his design in nineteen forty-six. Goldman filed for a similar one.
National Public Radio says that after a dispute, Watson received the patent and Goldman received a license to make the cart.
Sources differ on the exact terms of that deal, so we will leave it there.
Here is our reading. Nested carts save space, and they are easier to move in a row.
A professor at the University of Leeds, Andrew Warnes, argues that carts, along with cars and home freezers, helped fuel impulse buying.
If you can carry more, you may buy more. That fits Goldman's own starting problem, but it is an argument, not a measured number.
Next time you take a cart from the line, look at the back. On many carts, the back of the basket swings open when another cart pushes into it.
That swinging gate traces back to the idea of the nesting design of the nineteen forties.
So the shopping cart began as something people refused. Now most of us cannot imagine a supermarket without one.
A good idea does not always sell itself. And some things we never question at all. Take the calendar on your wall.
Why does February have only twenty-eight days?
